bib.title: Food-101 – Mining Discriminative Components with Random Forests
bib.venue: ECCV 2014 (venue not printed in the PDF text; from the ledger)

question: How can pictured dishes be recognised automatically, and how does a Random Forest based discriminative component mining method perform on a new 101-class food dataset?
hypothesis: Mining discriminative image components (superpixel-aligned) jointly for all classes with Random Forests beats global classifiers and prior part-mining methods for food, where local components matter.
contributions: A novel discriminative part mining method based on Random Forests.
A superpixel-based patch sampling strategy that prevents running many detectors on sliding windows.
A novel, large scale and publicly available dataset for food recognition (Food-101).
Experiments showing the approach outperforms Improved Fisher Vectors and the part-based mining approach of [34] on Food-101.

method.summary: Food-101 is 101'000 foodspotting.com images in 101 dish classes (750 uncleaned train, 250 hand-cleaned test per class). The proposed RFDC method trains a Random Forest on superpixel features, selects distinctive leaves as components, trains a linear SVM per component, and classifies with spatially pooled component scores and a multi-class SVM. It is compared with BOW, IFV, RF, RCF, MLDS and a CNN.
method.task: food image classification (101 classes); also scene classification on MIT-Indoor

datasets.name: Food-101
datasets.split: 750 train and 250 test images per class
datasets.source: downloaded from foodspotting.com; top 101 most popular and consistently named dishes; publicly downloadable at vision.ee.ethz.ch/datasets/food-101/; licence not stated
datasets.preprocessing: Rescaled to maximum side length 512 pixels; smaller images excluded. Test images manually cleaned; training images deliberately not cleaned, so they contain some noise (intense colors, sometimes wrong labels). Noise rate not measured.

datasets.name: MIT-Indoor
datasets.size: approx. 80 train and 20 test images per class (restricted train set); also full train set
datasets.split: original protocol of Quattoni and Torralba; restricted train set and full train set, original test set
datasets.preprocessing: Training images horizontally flipped to produce more samples; 100'000 samples per bag

models.name: RFDC (Random Forest Discriminant Components)
models.architecture: Random Forest of SVM-split trees on superpixels, linear SVM per mined component, structured-output multi-class SVM on spatially pooled component scores

other.trees: 30 (comparison on Food-101: max depth 5; default in parameter study: mined at depth 7)
other.positives_per_component: 100 in parameter study; 500 in the Food-101 comparison
other.superpixels: graph-based superpixels of Felzenszwalb and Huttenlocher, sigma=0.1, k=300, min size 1% of image area; about 30 per image, about 2.4 million in training set
other.features: dense SURF (signed square-rooted) plus L*a*b color, also extracted in the superpixel bounding box; Improved Fisher Vectors with 64-mode GMM, PCA-whitened, concatenated into 8'576 values
other.spatial_pooling: spatial pyramid with 3 levels, each superpixel fully contributes to each region it is part of, scores averaged

models.name: CNN (architecture of Krizhevsky et al. 2012, Caffe)

other.training: trained on Food-101 until converged (450'000 iterations); six days on an NVIDIA Tesla K20X; initialisation not stated

models.name: BOW, IFV, RF, RCF, MLDS
models.architecture: BOW: dense SURF, 1024 k-means clusters, 3-level spatial pyramid; IFV: Improved Fisher Vectors with spatial pyramid, parameters as in [19]; RF: forest used directly for classification; RCF: Randomized Clustering Forests of [29]; MLDS: re-implementation of [34] with superpixels instead of sliding HOG patches

other.MLDS: negative set 500'000 random superpixels; discovery set one class (about 22'500); k-means clusters/samples ratio 1/3; at most 10 iterations; each SVM trained on top 10 members; 20 components per class

training.objective: Random Forest node splits maximise information gain I(S,phi)=H(S)-(|Sl|/|S| H(Sl)+|Sr|/|S| H(Sr)) with class entropy; component models are linear binary SVMs with iterative hard-negative mining; final classifier is a structured-output multi-class SVM (optimized cutting plane algorithm, DLib)
training.hardware: CNN: NVIDIA Tesla K20X; RFDC: CPU, 8 cores at test time
training.compute: RFDC full pipeline about 250 cpu hours (including vocabulary training, i/o etc.); about 55% on forest, 15% on component models, 20% on final classifier; CNN six days on one K20X

other.forest_sampling: 200'000 of the 2.4M superpixels held out as validation set; each tree grown on 200'000 random superpixels from the remaining 2.2M
other.node_splits: 100 random binary class partitions per node, one SVM per partition, the one maximising Eq. 1 kept; SVM trained on at most 20'000 superpixels; splitting stops if a node has fewer than 25 samples
other.component_selection: distinctiveness(l|y)=sum_s delta(l,s) p(y|s); non-maxima suppression drops leaves sharing more than half the same superpixels with a better leaf; top N leaves per class

inference.samples: single run; no repeats or seeds reported

other.classification_time: about 0.8 seconds per image on 8 cores (MIT-Indoor settings), 70% encoding, 25% evaluating part models

metrics.name: Average accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of test images that are correctly classified

baselines: MIT-Indoor part-based and global methods from the literature
eval.protocol: Food-101: 750 train / 250 test per class, one accuracy per method, no confidence intervals or repeats. Parameter study varies one dimension at a time from defaults. MIT-Indoor: original protocol.

evidence.quote: On purpose, the training images were not cleaned, and thus still contain some amount of noise.

results.claim: RFDC reaches 50.76% average accuracy on Food-101, ahead of IFV and MLDS but behind the CNN.
results.setup: Food-101, 750 train / 250 test per class, 30 trees, max depth 5, 500 positives per component, 20 components per class
results.table: Table 2, row rfdc (this paper), column Avg. Acc. [%]

results.claim: The CNN outperforms RFDC by 5.64 points, at the cost of six days of training on a Tesla K20X.
results.setup: Food-101, AlexNet-style CNN (Krizhevsky et al.) trained in Caffe until converged (450'000 iterations)
results.quote: cnn set the state of the art and rfdc are outperformed by a margin of 5.64%. This is paid by a considerably longer training time of six days on a nvidia Tesla K20X.

results.claim: IFV, the best global non-CNN classifier, scores 38.88% on Food-101; BOW scores 28.51%.
results.setup: Food-101, same split, spatial pyramid, multi-class SVM
results.table: Table 2, row ifv [32], column Avg. Acc. [%]
results.note: Text says IFV beats BOW by 10%.

results.claim: MLDS (re-implementation of Singh et al. with superpixels) scores 42.63%, 3.75 points above IFV.
results.table: Table 2, row mlds, column Avg. Acc. [%]
results.note: Text: improvement of 3.75% with respect to ifv.

results.claim: Using the Random Forest directly for classification (RF) gives 32.72% and Randomized Clustering Forests 28.46%, no better than BOW, so mining plus component SVMs matter.
results.table: Table 2, row rf [3], column Avg. Acc. [%]

results.claim: RFDC gains 8.13 points over MLDS and 11.88 points over IFV.
results.setup: Food-101, RFDC 50.76 versus IFV 38.88 and MLDS 42.63
results.quote:
we measure an accuracy of 50.76%, an improvement of 8.13% and 11.88% com-
pared to mlds and ifv, respectively.

results.claim: On the full classifier, IFV SURF@64 plus Color@64 features give RFDC 49.40% under the default parameter-study settings; HOG gives only 8.85%.
results.setup: Food-101, RFDC with default settings (30 trees, depth 7, top 20 components, 100 positives), varying the feature encoding
results.table: Table 1, row ifv surf@64 + Color@64, column Avg. Acc. [%]
results.note: Table 1 prints 49.40 for this configuration, whereas Table 2 prints 50.76 for the comparison settings (depth 5, 500 positives); the paper does not explain the 1.36 point gap.

results.claim: Accuracy saturates with components per class: going from 20 to 50 components raises feature dimension from 42'420 to 106'050 for a modest gain.
results.quote:
from 42’420 for 20 components, the dimensionality reaches 106’050 for 50
components

results.claim: On MIT-Indoor RFDC reaches 54.40% with the restricted train set and 58.36% with the full train set, below IFV (60.77) and DMS (64.03).
results.setup: MIT-Indoor, 50 components per class, 100'000 samples per bag, flipped training images
results.quote:
our method yields
54.40% and 58.36% average accuracy for the restricted and full training set

results.claim: Full RFDC training takes around 250 CPU hours and classifying one image takes about 0.8 seconds on 8 cores.
results.setup: MIT-Indoor settings, full pipeline including vocabulary training and i/o
results.quote:
our full pipeline uses around
250 cpu hours

results.claim: Food-101 training images are deliberately uncleaned and contain some label noise, but the noise rate is not measured; only the 250 test images per class were manually cleaned.
results.note: No percentage, audit, annotator count or cleaning criteria are given.

limits: Training-set noise (wrong labels, intense colors) is acknowledged but never quantified; test cleaning procedure (who, criteria, number removed) is not described.

Single run per method with no seeds, repeats or significance test; the CNN baseline is an AlexNet-era model trained from scratch (initialisation not stated), a strong 2012 baseline that has since been far surpassed.
No code or weights released; only the dataset.
On MIT-Indoor the method does not match DMS (restricted train set) and is below IFV.

figures.caption: Overview of our component mining. A Random Forest is used to hierarchically cluster superpixels of the training set. Then, discriminative clusters of superpixels in the leaves are selected and used to train the component models. After mining, the rf is not used anymore.
figures.why: Shows the three-stage pipeline in one picture.

figures.caption: Classification performance measured for the evaluated methods. All component mining approaches use 20 components per class.
One example for 100 out of the 101 classes in our dataset.
figures.why: Shows the variation and look-alike classes in the dataset.
